title: Prediction Is Not Fact
outcome: By the end, I can keep predicted and observed outcomes separate and audit a disagreement.
scenario: A fictional drying trial uses a fixed rule and later measures what actually happened.
given: Model D predicts slow when moisture score is at least 5; quick otherwise.
Observation policy: slow if drying takes above 8 minutes; quick otherwise. Trial T has score 4 and measured time 9 minutes.

steps.label: Predict
steps.detail: 4 is below 5, so D predicts quick.

steps.label: Observe later
steps.detail: Measured time is 9 minutes; above 8 means observed slow.

steps.label: Compare evidence
steps.detail: Prediction quick disagrees with observation slow.

explanation: The moisture score generates a prediction; it is not the observed drying time. The later measurement supplies separate evidence under the stated observation policy. Save both values and their units. Altering the recorded time to match D would destroy the evaluation rather than repair the model.

counterfactual.change: Keep score 4 but measure exactly 8 minutes.
counterfactual.prediction: The observed label becomes quick and agrees with the prediction.
counterfactual.reason: Above 8 is strict: equality is quick under this policy.

student_task: Which field changes the observation label, and which field changes the model prediction?
teacher_answer: Time changes the observation; moisture score changes the prediction. At score 4 and time 8, both labels are quick.
project_evidence: In sorter trials, record predicted categories before collecting reference evidence, then retain disagreements for investigation.
limits: One failure does not prove every prediction is wrong; one agreement does not establish reliability on future trials.
review_note: New fictional worked case reviewed against the weekly topic and reserved independent assessment. Keep that assessment separate; this picture is supported practice.
